content: The cost of implementing a single serological assay for hepatitis testing would at least double the expenses. A survey conducted across 19 lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) revealed that a single serological assay testing strategy, primarily using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), is being utilized in various hospital-based services. These include blood donor screening, harm-reduction services, and HIV treatment and care clinics. Implementation Considerations for Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) and Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) Antibody Testing: 1. Selection of Assays: While RDTs generally have lower analytical sensitivity compared to EIAs, it is crucial to select assays with minimal false-positive rates. Chapter 15 provides detailed guidance on setting up laboratory services, selecting assays, and ensuring quality in hepatitis testing. 2. Although many EIAs and chemiluminescent immunoassays (CLIAs) are commercially available, there is a lack of HBsAg RDTs that meet minimum performance, safety, and quality standards. National regulatory authorities are responsible for approving RDTs for use after assessing their quality, safety, and performance. 3. Accurate Testing: All hepatitis B and C testing should follow the assay manufacturer’s instructions, including an HBsAg neutralization step if applicable. Standard operating procedures (SOPs) and job aids can help minimize errors in testing and reporting, thereby improving result quality. 4. Staff Training and Supervision: Testing environments should adhere to quality management systems and employ qualified, proficient, and motivated laboratory staff trained in performing various assays. Health-care workers must understand the strengths and limitations of testing strategies, counsel patients appropriately, and act on both positive and negative results. 5. Linkage to Care: Since some preliminary results may be false positives, appropriate linkage to additional testing and clinical evaluation is necessary, especially in outreach programs. Retesting strategies should be implemented for individuals at high risk of acquiring HCV. 6. On-Site Testing: Providing nucleic acid testing (NAT) or HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) testing at the same site as serological testing is optimal. This approach enables rapid turnaround, reduces loss to follow-up, and minimizes personal and health-care costs associated with referrals to distant centers. Research Gaps in HBsAg and HCV Antibody Testing: The diagnostic performance, cost, and cost-effectiveness of one-assay versus two-assay serological testing strategies for HBsAg or HCV antibodies in diverse settings need to be assessed. Validation of EIAs and RDTs using less invasive sample collection methods, such as oral fluid, capillary whole blood, and dried blood spots (DBS), is necessary. WHO Recommendations for Managing Chronic Hepatitis B: Monitoring and Treatment Decisions: The persistence of HBsAg for six months or more defines chronic hepatitis B (CHB). Decisions on treatment initiation are based on clinical features, ALT levels, and HBV DNA concentrations. Where HBV DNA testing is unavailable, treatment may be considered based on persistently abnormal ALT levels alone, after excluding other causes of elevated ALT such as impaired glucose tolerance, dyslipidemia, and fatty liver. Who to Treat: Treatment is prioritized for individuals with CHB and clinical evidence of compensated or decompensated cirrhosis, regardless of ALT levels, HBeAg status, or HBV DNA levels. Treatment is also recommended for adults with CHB aged over 30 years, with persistently abnormal ALT levels and high HBV DNA levels (>20,000 IU/mL), even in the absence of cirrhosis. Who Not to Treat: Antiviral therapy is not recommended for individuals with minimal liver disease or fibrosis, persistently normal ALT levels, and low HBV DNA levels (<2,000 IU/mL). These individuals require regular monitoring to assess disease progression and determine the need for future treatment. Monitoring During and After Treatment: Regular monitoring of ALT, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels is recommended, with more frequent assessments during the first year of treatment or in individuals with advanced liver disease. Monitoring adherence to therapy is critical. After treatment discontinuation, monitoring is essential to detect reactivation and determine the need for retreatment. Challenges in LMICs: Limited access to HBV DNA testing in LMICs poses a significant barrier to effective CHB management. In such settings, decisions to initiate treatment rely on clinical features and ALT levels alone. Integration of routine monitoring for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) alongside disease progression monitoring is recommended to improve outcomes. Conclusion: Regular monitoring and timely treatment initiation are essential to prevent disease progression and improve patient outcomes.
